Operator: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen, and welcome to today's Legrand's 2026 half year results conference call. For your information, this conference is being recorded. All participants are in a listen-only mode. Later, there will be a question-and-answer session. At this time, I would like to hand the call over to CEO, Mr. Benoît Coquart, and CFO, Mr. Franck Lemery. Please go ahead, sir.

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): Thank you very much. Good morning, everybody. Franck, Renaud, and myself are happy to welcome you to Legrand H1 2026 conference call and webcast. This morning, as usual, we published our press release, financial statements, and the slideshow that we will refer to during the call. After a few opening remarks, we will comment on the results in more details. Let me start on page four with the key highlights of the quarter. First, Legrand delivered another period of record sales growth together with continued excellent profitability. Second, we are continuing to implement our 2030 strategic roadmap with determination. Third, we are raising our full year 2026 targets. Moving to pages six and seven, I will start with an overview of sales. Sales delivered strong growth of +17.4% in H1 2026, excluding currency effect, comprising first, an organic growth of +9.8%, driven by data centers and energy transition-related offerings.
Second, growth from acquisitions with a positive scope effect of +6.9%. Based on acquisitions announced and the likely date of consolidation, the overall impact of acquisitions would be around +8% for the full year. The exchange rate effect was -3.7% in H1. Based on average exchange rates in June 2026, the full-year currency effect would be around -1.5%. On page seven, you will find the key takeaways by geographies on a like-for-like basis. Europe saw sales down -2.4% in a building market that remains as expected contrasted. North and Central America increased sharply by +24.2%, driven by strong success of data center and energy transition solutions in the U.S. Lastly, rest of the world grew by +2.3% in the first half, with significant growth in India, Australia, and several other Asian countries, while activity in China remained soft.
Despite the geopolitical situation, sales in the Middle East grew in H1. These were the main comments I wanted to make on sales. I will now hand over to Franck for more color on our financial performance.

Franck Lemery (CFO, Legrand): Thank you, Benoît. Good morning to all of you. I will start on page eight with adjusted operating profit. Profitability, despite inflationary pressure, remained very strong in H1 2026, with an adjusted operating margin of 20.8%. This is a high level reflecting strong execution and adaptability, notably effective pricing and cost productivity, as well as the quality of our recent acquisitions. Going now to page nine regarding value creation. First, net profit reached EUR 698 million, up +11.2% versus H1 2025. This increase was driven primarily by higher operating profit, a slightly lower corporate income tax of 27.5%, and the negative evolution of the financial results. Second, free cash flow came to EUR 488 million, representing 9% of sales. This is it for the key financial topics. I'm now handing over back to Benoît.

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): Thank you, Franck. During the first half of the year, we actively deployed a strategic roadmap. Let's take three examples: data centers, acquisitions, and innovation. First, data centers on page 11. The group's strong organic growth in the first half was driven in particular by its data center business, which delivered organic growth of above +30% and now accounts for 32% of Legrand's revenue. Legrand has built one of the broadest offerings in the industry, from on-site power generation to installation testing. Its portfolio includes more than 140,000 product references and a growing range of services, including engineering services, on-site support, testing, and commissioning. The group is particularly well-positioned to support the development of high-density AI data centers through scalable, highly engineered solutions tailored to the specific needs of hyperscalers, colocation, new cloud providers, and enterprise customers. Second example, acquisitions on page 13.
Far in 2026, we already announced seven acquisitions so far, including one today in Finland. All are focused in energy and digital transition, further strengthening the group's leadership positions in high-growth markets. They represent a combined annual revenue of around EUR 450 million throughout the world. Third example, innovation on pages 15 and 16. As you know, innovation and regular new product launches have always been and remain a key priority for Legrand. You can see once again our continuous strong innovation momentum with the numerous product launches in all verticals since the beginning of the year. We can now move to page 18 with our full-year 2026 targets. Confident in our action plans, we are raising our full-year 2026 targets. Based on its first half performance and the current global macroeconomic environment, Legrand is now targeting the following in 2026.
Sales growth, excluding currency effects of between +16% and +19%, versus +10% and +15% previously. Comprising organic growth of between +8% and +10%, versus +4% and +7% previously, and growth through acquisitions of around +8%, versus between +6% and +8% previously. Adjusted operating margin after acquisitions of between 20.5% and 21% of sales, unchanged. CSR achievement rate of at least 100% for the second year of its 2025, 2027 roadmap. In conclusion, this first half highlights the strength of our business model and the acceleration of our momentum, strong growth, high profitability and discipline execution. Our capital market day on September 29, 2026 in Singapore will be an opportunity to provide an update on our 2030 ambitions, with a particular focus on data centers. We would be very happy to welcome you there.
Those were the key topics of this release. I suggest that we switch now to Q&A. Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. To ask a question, please press star one and one on your telephone and wait for your name to be announced. To withdraw your question, please press star one and one again. To give more people the opportunity to ask questions, please limit yourselves to one question and one follow-up. We thank you for your understanding. One moment for our first question. We will now take our first question from Andre Kukhnin from UBS. Please ask your question. Andre, your line is open.

Andre Kukhnin (Analyst, UBS): Yes, good morning. Thank you very much for taking my questions. Could we just start with comments on the data center-specific growth in the second half, if you could specify that for Americas and maybe the rest of the world as well, please?

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): Well. In the first half, as I said, the data center business grew a little bit more than +30% on a worldwide basis, with a growth which was stronger in North America than elsewhere. As far as the full year is concerned, you know that three months back, we were guiding for close to 20%. Now we believe that the full year basis, our data center will grow between 25% and 30%, organically for the full year. Which you can do the math, but basically it means in H2, which would be between 20% and 30%. We expect to see the continuation of the strong growth in data center. I have to say that the pace is not slowing down. We have very, very solid orders. A lot of discussions going on, we are quite optimistic, I have to say, for the next couple of months.

Andre Kukhnin (Analyst, UBS): Got it. Thank you. If I may just ask, I think during the quarter you talked about working on the sidecar offering for the future 800 VDC architectures. Could you talk about how long have you been working on that, and when do you expect that to be commercially available? Given that, I think this is seen as a sort of a transfer step between the current architectures and the full solid-state setups. Do you also intend to have an offering for what I think is going to be the battery rack in the full 800 VDC?

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): Well, Andre, I expected to have more questions on the results before getting into the LVDC topic, which the financial community is sort of obsessed by. I don't want to be too exhaustive on that because we have a CMD end of September. We'll spend a day together, it will be the opportunity to go a lot deeper into those topics than during a call dedicated to the results. To make a long story short, yes, we are working on the full hybrid architecture including the sidecar, we are not late compared to what we can see on the market. Yes, of course, we are also working on the next step, which is a full LVDC, even though there's now a consensus on the market that it won't come before some time.
I remind you the sort of base scenario in which we work, which is that the so-called hybrid architecture. With AC-DC architecture could represent as much as maybe 10% or 20% of the new IT loads by 2030. As far as the full LVDC is concerned, now most people expect that it would represent at best 1% or 2% of the new IT loads by 2030. Those are the orders of magnitude that we've been talking about for almost a year now, I can only note that more and more people are on the same page as us. Yes, we are working on both architecture, hybrid architecture and LVDC, to answer your question. Once again, we'll give you a lot more color in September, I hope, Andre, you will join us in Singapore.

Andre Kukhnin (Analyst, UBS): Of course. Yeah, we'll be there. Thank you very much for taking the question.

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): Thank you.

Andre Kukhnin (Analyst, UBS): Okay.

Operator: Thank you. We will now take our next question, and our next question comes from the line of Phil Buller of JPMorgan. Please ask your question. Phil, your line is open.

Phil Buller (Analyst, JPMorgan): Hi. Good morning. Thank you for the question. I'd like to start with another one on data center, if I may. It's 32% of your sales now, which is great on the one hand, but there are these growing concerns about a potential bubble or at least the medium to longer term affordability of it all. Perhaps you can share what you're seeing on the ground in terms of the medium-term outlook. Are you concerned internally by the risk of a potential bubble beyond that near-term optimism? Just to start there, please.

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): Well, I've not heard much about a bubble as far the AI was concerned. I heard a lot about a bubble concerning potential valuations. What we see on the ground is that there's a huge demand, which is not slowing down at all. A sort of race to capacity, which is happening, with orders coming to be delivered in 2026, some of them in 2027, some of them in 2028. Frankly speaking, when I see the penetration rates of AI, which is still very low, and the disruption potential it has on so many sectors, name software, traveling, financial services, health, and many others, I think that we are just scratching the surface of what AI can bring as a benefit. If we think that AI will be almost everywhere and will impact all sectors, then you need a lot more computing capacities than is currently available.
I'm not saying that we will grow 30% forever. We won't, of course. I still see a very positive momentum for a couple of years. Here again, we'll try to give you a bit more color on what we see ahead of us in terms of gigawatt, market growth, and so on, in September. Again, I don't see a reason why, given the low penetration rate of AI in many sectors, why the need for computing capabilities would slow down.

Phil Buller (Analyst, JPMorgan): That makes sense, and it's very clear. Thank you. My follow-up is on the margin topic, really. Clearly a solid performance in Q2 or H1, given what's going on in the world. By geography, it's really the U.S. that's driving that, or North America, I assume driven by the data center leverage. Perhaps you can talk to the margins in Europe and the rest of the world year-on-year. How should we think about that evolution in the second half in the context of the unchanged margin? Are there any AI benefits that you can touch on that you're able to achieve internally as well? Thanks.

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): Well, as far as margin is concerned, what happened in H1 is pretty clear. You can see that we have 20 points decrease in operating margin, which is coming half organic, half basis points, sorry, 20 basis point decrease, half from acquisition, half organic, with gross margin, which is down 130 basis points coming mostly from acquisitions. You know that the company we are acquiring tend to have a lower gross margin and lower SG&A base than the rest of the business. SG&A, which has a positive impact of 90 basis points on our profitability, which is mostly leveraged. Other, which has a slight positive impact of 20 basis points with a level of restructuring in million euros, which is similar to H1. This is for the group.
Of course, NCA, North and Central America, has a very strong performance, which makes a lot of sense given the strong sales growth they are experiencing. It compensates the decrease in Europe and in the rest of the world, which is suffering from softer sales. You know, especially that in Europe, we are more integrated. Europe is bearing a number of central costs, holding costs, as well as global centers for innovation. When you don't have top-line impact in Europe, it has, of course, a negative impact on profitability. This is for H1. No surprise, more or less a stable margin, let's say, with lower gross margin, positive impact from SG&A and slight positive impact from others. As far as H2 is concerned, frankly speaking, we'll see. It will depend on the top-line evolution we will have in the three areas.
The bottom line is that we are confirming that despite inflation of purchase price, despite muted sales in Europe, despite the geopolitical situation, which remains somehow uncertain, we are fully confirming of our guidance in margin, i.e., an adjusted profit margin of between 20.5% and 21%. Again, to see the difference from one zone to another, let's wait for H2 to happen and let's wait for especially the top-line in H2 to happen before commenting.

Phil Buller (Analyst, JPMorgan): Thank you. Thanks.

Operator: Thank you. We will now proceed to the next question, Our next question comes from Daniela Costa of Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead, Daniela. Your line is open.

Daniela Costa (Analyst, Goldman Sachs): Hi. Good morning. I will start my question and then I'll ask the follow-up after. On the following up on this point on pricing into the second half, I guess that's within your realm of control. If you could give us any idea of whether you've done any price increases in July or

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): Yeah

Daniela Costa (Analyst, Goldman Sachs): do you see and especially differentiating between data centers and the rest would be very useful.

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): Yeah. Well, it's difficult to differentiate from one zone to another, from one business to another. I can give you the global numbers. Our price effect was + 2.9% in H1. You can see the acceleration between Q1 and Q2. Q1 was at + 2.1%, Q2 was at + 3.6%, and globally + 2.9% for H1. Given the environment, especially the purchase price environment, we now expect a price effect for the full year, which could be up to around + 3%. Having in mind that the pricing phase started in H2 last year. The basic comparison in terms of pricing is a bit more demanding. We were expecting three months back to be between + 2% and + 3%, and we are now confirming to be around + 3%, given the environment.
If the situation of purchase price, so price of raw components was to worsen for whatever reason, of course, we would keep our ability to do a bit more pricing. When we entered the year, we thought we would do + 1% to + 2%. We are shooting for + 3%, and if it was needed, we could do more. This was for selling price. As far as purchase price is concerned, I can also give you the data. In H1, it was + 3% purchase price, + 2% in Q1, + 4% in Q2, and we are now expecting an inflation to be probably a little bit higher than + 4%. Expectations for the full year, purchase price of + 4% plus, let's say, and selling price of about + 3% excluding tariff. This is what we are shooting for.
Should we need to do more selling price, we would do more depending on the environment.

Daniela Costa (Analyst, Goldman Sachs): Thank you. Just as a follow-up in terms of the data center business, we are starting to see some announcements in Europe. I think we saw SoftBank in France, there has been others. I know that your portfolio is slightly different in Europe versus the U.S., how should we think about this? Should we just imagine you benefiting the same way you did in the U.S., or there are some things we should keep in mind on the differences in the portfolio?

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): Well, no benefit yet in 2026 so far because of the time difference between announcement and actual data center setup. You know that because of permitting, because of access to electricity, access to the grid, it can take up to three, four, five years before a project is announced and the time the data center is effectively open, we are late cycle in data center. We start to do some sales a few months before a data center is open. We are not yet seeing the same amount of business as we see in the U.S. It is not specific to Legrand. I mean, it is a whole market. Our core assumption is that it should help us in the years to come. So far in 2026, the most exciting market, faster growing, remains the U.S.
The day it will come bigger scale in Europe, it will be a good news because theoretically, we have the ability to sell more dollar per megawatt in Europe than in the U.S., because there are a number of product families that we have in Europe and not in the U.S. It would be a good news, but we are not seeing that yet. The vast majority of our business, of the market, and of the growth is still coming from the U.S.

Daniela Costa (Analyst, Goldman Sachs): Got it. Thank you.

Operator: We will now proceed to take our next question. Our next question comes from the line of George Featherstone of Barclays. Please ask your question. George, your line is open.

George Featherstone (Analyst, Barclays): Morning, everyone. Thanks for taking the question. First one would just be on the non-data center business and kind of a little bit of an update about what you're seeing there and what you're implying for the rest of the year in terms of that non-data center business and the growth embedded in that. Thanks.

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): We're obviously seeing an improvement between Q1 and Q2 in the building market. The underlying building markets remain not very supportive, and this is the case both in the U.S. and Europe, which is not a surprise again. From the very beginning, we told you that, especially in Europe, the statistics were supposed to show us some market improvement, but that it wouldn't come before the end of the year, and that it still had to be demonstrated. It's not a surprise, but no improvement between Q1 and Q2. The good news, if I may say, that within this building market, which remains somehow a bit depressed, we see a number of product families, especially those related to energy transition, which are doing better than the traditional so-called essential product families. All products related to the electrification.
For us, it's transformer, circuit breakers, measure, load shedding, and a few others. are a few points better than light switches, lighting, AV, floor boxes, and all this kind of stuff. It showed that even in a difficult building environment, we have some businesses that have the ability to over-perform the market. What will it be for the rest of the year? If we listen to specialists, most people expect the U.S. building market to remain quite depressed. There's no short-term positive signals coming from the experts, especially in resi, even though it's less than 10% of our sales now in the U.S. Nobody expect the resi market to rebound in 2026. Most experts believe that Europe should progressively improve, with a number of uncertainties related to consumer confidence, geopolitics, the cost of energy, blah, blah, but at a slow pace.
This is a sort of macro scenario. What have we included into our guidance? As you could see, we have included data center market, strong growth, 25%-30% like for like, and the rest of the business growing low single digit as it grew in H1. We haven't incorporated into our guidance a sharp rebound in the building market, neither in the U.S. nor in Europe.

George Featherstone (Analyst, Barclays): Okay. That's really helpful. Thank you. Then just a couple of follow-ups on the data center conversations you've been having.

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): Yep.

George Featherstone (Analyst, Barclays): First one would be, you spoke about confidence in the demand outlook. Are you able to put some context around that? Maybe give us a growth rate you're seeing in orders. Is it above the sales growth rate, for example? Then the second thing on your acquisitions you've made there recently. There's perhaps a consistent theme forming, which is you're buying more businesses within the testing and commissioning space. Can you perhaps talk to the opportunity that you're seeing there? Thank you.

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): Well, I'm not sure I can give you a lot more color on the data center growth by geography, by customers, by product types. I can maybe tell you that if you look at the product families, of course, when you grow more than 30%, it means that you have some product families growing 50%, 60%, 70%, 100%. Those growing the most are probably cooling, testing, commissioning, and part of the powertrain. They correspond to some of the acquisitions we've made in the last two or three years. Again, we are seeing a very good growth and very solid order inflow across most of our product families. As far as the latest acquisitions are concerned, well, the objective was to build significant market position in critical power in the U.S.
For those of you who know Legrand for quite some time, you know that we've been trying to enter the energy transition/critical power in the U.S. for quite some time. This was a market which was occupied by big guys. For years we didn't find the right way to enter. Well, interestingly, data centers provide us a very good entry point. We've bought a number of companies active in powertrain. Power generation with turbine packaged in a container on site to do power generation whenever there's a actually as a backup power or as a main generator. Medium voltage with gear, low voltage with gear, busway, busbar, testing and commissioning. The whole powertrain. What is of interest is that most of the acquisitions have something like half of their sales in data center and half of their sales in the other type of verticals.
Could be building, could be renewables, could be infra, could be industries, could be health. By entering into the critical power in the U.S., we also enter into other verticals, and we have started to build a meaningful and significant position in energy transition in those other verticals. It's not only about testing and commissioning, it's mostly about critical power in the U.S. It is a very interesting position, growing nicely and not only growing nicely in data centers, but also growing nicely in other verticals. If I zoom on testing and commissioning, well, Avtron, which is a company you referred to, is a world leader in load banks, has very strong market share in the U.S. and elsewhere. It will prove to be one of the most exciting acquisitions of Legrand. Very good multiple, very strong growth, very nice profitability.
Indeed, it is for us a way to be even more involved on the high density AI data center. When you have 1 GW, 2 GW, 3 GW data center, when you have a 1 MW rack, for example, which is liquid cooled, not only you need to test the loads, but you also need to test the liquid cooling systems. The higher the density, the more liquid cooled the data center, the more testing you need and the more commissioning you need and the more sales Legrand will do. It's a very interesting acquisition.

George Featherstone (Analyst, Barclays): Okay. Thanks a lot

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): I hope, George, that you will come in to Singapore because we'll have a more opportunity to discuss that, and we'll even display some upfront product, and we have some upfront people, so we'll be able to talk directly to them.

George Featherstone (Analyst, Barclays): I'll certainly see you there. Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. We will now take our next question from the line of Max Yates from Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead, Max. Your line is open.

Max Yates (Analyst, Morgan Stanley): Thank you. Maybe if I could just start on the margins. I noticed you had higher restructuring costs above the line this quarter. I just wanted to ask about some of the moving pieces. What is your expectation for restructuring as we go through the full year? Was that a temporary kind of higher restructuring of Europe, or is that something you expect to be higher for the full year and therefore a drag on margins? Then also, if you could comment on whether there were any tariff refunds during the quarter, because that's a consistent theme we've heard across a number of companies. Thank you.

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): As far as the restructuring is concerned, well, we're not much commenting by zone. At group level, we had a restructuring of EUR 33 million in H1, which was very much in line with what we had in H1 2025, because we had EUR 34 million restructuring in H1 2025. Yes, we remain very active. While it's not a surprise to see a lot of restructuring in Europe, because typically that's where we lack sales. When our volumes are not going, we tend, of course, to do restructuring, footprint optimization, blah, blah. As far as the full year is concerned, our main assumption in that it could be close in terms of million euros to 2025. I remind you that in 2025, it was EUR 65 million. I cannot commit on a precise number, but it will be around this number.
As far as the tariff refund is concerned, well, tariff has become a very complex issue, I have to admit. Even though we are tracking that very carefully, the potential refund, whether you ask it or not, new tariff, tariffs that are canceled, that are replayed, it has become a very complex topic. I have to say that in H1, tariff did not have a material impact, neither positive nor negative. That's it. If we can get a bit of refund, we will. Frankly speaking, it is not a strategic topic for us. It would be a one-time benefit, not huge. It is not a topic on which we are spending a lot of time. We are focusing a lot more in the U.S. on how can we cope with this data center hypergrowth, how can we better serve our customers, rather than on tariff.
We don't expect it to have a very meaningful impact, one way or the other, on the 2026 accounts.

Max Yates (Analyst, Morgan Stanley): No, sure. I was just trying to understand whether the margin was clean or not. The second question.

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): To answer, I can answer. Yes, the margins are clean.

Max Yates (Analyst, Morgan Stanley): Okay.

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): They will be clean for the full year.

Max Yates (Analyst, Morgan Stanley): The second question, and I think it was something kind of George was trying to get at, but I think you've previously talked about around six months visibility in your data center business. You kind of talked earlier in the call about some of your orders were now kind of extending into 2027 or maybe 2028. Could you maybe give us a feel of kind of how long your backlog is today? Has that meaningfully expanded? And any commentary on how much of your revenues for 2027 might already be locked in by your order backlog would be really helpful context. Thank you.

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): I don't really like this concept of 2027 being locked in by backlog, because we've been consistently telling you that backlog is more, for us, an indication of for which customer we have to serve and when, and which supply chain investments we have to make in order to make sure that we deliver properly, more than a leading indicator of what our sales in 2027 going to be. Because a backlog can be canceled, can be delayed, can be modified. Of course, we start to have orders for 2027. On some very specific businesses where the lead time are longer, we even have a few orders for 2028 and sometimes 2029. Does it give us a lot of visibility? The answer is no. Again, because we are not counting on this backlog to make our assumptions.
What give us confidence on the fact that the data center market will continue to grow, it's more the gigawatts that were announced for 2027, 2028 and beyond. There are tens and tens of gigawatts, and each time there is a gigawatt being built, I remind you that 1 GW, we could potentially sell EUR 2 billion- EUR 3 billion of sales for gigawatt. EUR 2 billion- EUR 3 billion per gigawatt. This is more these kind of leading indicators we are tracking rather than a backlog, because again, backlog can be changed.

Max Yates (Analyst, Morgan Stanley): Understood. By the way, thank you very-

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): The total CapEx from our customers. To this extent, the recent announcements from some of the hyperscalers on the fact that they were even increasing their CapEx plans for 2026, 2027, 2028, is quite good news for Legrand, of course.

Max Yates (Analyst, Morgan Stanley): Excellent. Thank you very much.

Operator: We will now proceed to our next question. Our next question comes from Alasdair Leslie from Bernstein. Please ask your question, Alasdair. Your line is open.

Alasdair Leslie (Analyst, Bernstein): Thank you. Good morning, everyone. I wanted to follow up, I suppose, on what you were discussing previously around U.S. data center acquisitions, but maybe focusing more on the Girtz acquisition, your strategy there, but perhaps more in the context of how you're looking at the opportunity in prefabricated modular data centers now. Is the plan to develop dedicated Legrand power pods and maybe even modular IT pods? Maybe also if you could reflect on how this fits in with that partnership you have with Siemens and Cadolto in, I guess maybe that's focused more on Europe. Maybe you could confirm that. If you have any kind of estimate on how big the modular prefabricated market in the U.S. is right now, perhaps as a share of additions. Thank you.

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): No, it is a fact that the prefab, even though within this world you have different type of systems, is gaining ground because it helps our customers to optimize their supply chain and to open faster data centers. It's gaining ground worldwide. We do have already modular capabilities in a number of geographies. In the U.S., for example, we are able to provide genset modules with Girtz indeed, which are gas-powered or diesel-powered and which can be used even as a main source of power, especially in zones such as Texas and elsewhere. We are also providing skids, pre-mounted critical power powertrain with Kratos in the U.S. In Colombia, we have a unit fully dedicated to modules, which is called Tecnica. In Europe, we have a couple of units doing that, especially a new unit in Ireland called TES, and so on and so forth.
In Malaysia, we just acquired SRS, which has the ability to do skids and modules for power, medium voltage and low voltage. We have progressively acquired a number of capabilities to do modules. Not to mention our ability to do full HAC, hot aisle containment, including racks, busway, type of boxes and so on. We do have these capabilities, not everywhere, but at least in the U.S., in Southeast Asia, and in Europe. It's part of the nice growth we have. It's not the only one. That's it. I don't know what else I can tell you, except that once again, I will invite you to come to Singapore. I feel that it probably is the right time to do a CMD dedicated to data centers, given the number of questions we have.
Again, you have the ability to talk face-to-face to the teams in charge of all those businesses, and they will give you as much information as you want on those modules, skids, prefabricated product lines, and customer expectations.

Alasdair Leslie (Analyst, Bernstein): Yeah, great. I'll look forward to that. Thank you, Benoît. Thank you.

Operator: We will now take our next question. Our next question comes from Gael de-Bray from Deutsche Bank. Please go ahead, Gael, your line is open.

Gael de-Bray (Analyst, Deutsche Bank): Thanks. Thank you very much. Can I get back maybe to the question around the company's execution during the quarter? If there were any specific challenges beyond the price-cost dynamics that you've met to deliver that very strong growth in the quarter? Why specifically did you see both margins and free cash flow trending a bit down on the year-on-year basis? Whether you expect that to reverse maybe more positively into the second half? That's question number one.

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): If I have to name one operating challenge, it would definitely be how to cope with the hypergrowth of our data center business. Not to say that we have any margin issue on data center, but our teams are spending a lot of time optimizing the supply chain, speeding up development process of new product, shipping on time, sending people on site to help the installation and commissioning, and so on and so forth. It has clearly been a challenge. Did it have an impact on cost? Yes, probably. Our cost is not as optimized as if we're growing 10%. When you grow 30%+, which again means 50%, 60%, 70% in some geographies and in some product families, it comes with a number of additional costs. Again, it's pretty good news for Legrand.
As far as the difference between Q1 and Q2, I will let maybe Franck to give you more color.

Franck Lemery (CFO, Legrand): Especially on the cash flow, Gael, good morning. The question you ask. Cash flow at the end of H1 is at 9%. H1 is always soft. 9% is not unusual, and you know very well why it is soft. At 9%, it is not unusual if I look back at the last years, almost one year out of two was below or equal to 9%. It is a little bit soft on the back of higher working capital requirements, which are around 14%, where the typical working capital requirement for the group would be 12%. One third of that is totally mechanical, scope, conversion, all that. Two third is, I wouldn't call that company execution, but the current backdrop, which is a little bit more inventory, a little bit more account receivable, and also on the opposite, a little bit more accountable.
All that is the current picture. Looking ahead on the full year basis, we really think that working cap will be normalized and accordingly, a full year of free cash flow should be the usual one between 13%-15%. H1 is challenging, of course, in terms of managing the strong growth in data center. But whether in terms of margin or in terms of cash flow, nothing special, and we are confirming for the profitability of 20.5%-21%, yearly guidance, and we are confirming for the free cash flow, the 13%-15% long-term guidance.

Gael de-Bray (Analyst, Deutsche Bank): Understood. The second question is on the willingness to design and to launch a power sidecar offering for 2027. I was wondering whether you have, in your M&A pipeline today any specific targets in the rectifiers or battery backup segments?

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): You will understand that I cannot be too specific on our M&A pipeline. I will just answer that we have either internally or through contract manufacturing and subcontracting, all the technical building blocks of a sidecar. It might not be very obvious from the outside, but we have a lot of expertise in DC, in conversion. We are a UPS player, even though not a big one in data center, but we are a UPS player. We have, of course, a lot of capabilities in racking. So we have all the technological bricks, again, either organically or through subcontracting that we need to do a sidecar. Which, by the way, is not technologically speaking, something very complicated. Again, if your question is will you guys continue to do acquisitions in the quarters to come? The answer is yes.
Probably not at the same pace as the one we have had so far, which is almost a deal a month. We continue to have a very large pipeline of opportunities in data center and elsewhere. Again, I cannot be too specific on the countries or products, but we have a very large pipeline, and we will continue to do nice deals at a very reasonable price. Maybe worth mentioning, you didn't ask the question, Gael, but I know that you have the question in the back of your mind. We can add that the seven deals we have made so far in 2026 were paid less than 11 times 2025 EBIT. Probably less than 10 times 2026 EBIT. It remains quite reasonable.

Gael de-Bray (Analyst, Deutsche Bank): Impressive indeed. Thanks very much.

Operator: Thank you. We will now take our next question from the line of Martin Wilkie from Citi. Please ask your question, Martin. Your line is open.

Martin Wilkie (Analyst, Citi): Thank you. Good morning. It's Martin at Citi. The question is just to come back to acquisitions. You increased your acquisition impact guidance for the year. Just to check to start with, is that just based on the deals that you've already done? You list out a number that haven't yet been consolidated, or you've said, obviously, the pace might slow a bit in coming months. Just to check if that guidance includes some future deals or just based on what you've already done so far. That's the first question.

Franck Lemery (CFO, Legrand): No, it's based on what we have already done so far. There's no uncertainty. Let's say it could be 7.7, it could be 8.2, of course, but there's no uncertainty. The only uncertainty is how fast we'll be able to consolidate them. We will continue to make deals, but of course, if we close the deal in October, for example, or in November, you won't have much sales flowing into our 2026 P&L. The 8% parameter is based on the deals which have been announced so far, and should more deals come, they will more impact the 2027 parameter than 2026.

Martin Wilkie (Analyst, Citi): Thanks. That sort of leads on to my follow-on, because I think you're now at 32% of sales to data center, and I believe in the past you said that you wouldn't really want it to go above around 40%, which a while ago seemed like a distant prospect. Now, if you're adding a mid-single digit percent to top line each year through acquisitions, many in data center, and that end market is clearly growing much faster than everything else, it's not impossible that you get to 40% of sales in data center sort of within the next couple of years. Is that a ceiling that you still see, or how should we think about how you're looking at the portfolio on a sort of two or three-year view in terms of how big data center could become? Thank you.

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): Well, if I were you, I would save this question for the CMD, because it's more a long-term question than a short-term one. Yes, of course, if the data center business continue to grow much faster than the rest, and if we keep doing a lot of acquisitions in data center, it could be more than that, could be more than 40%. To commence, number one, not all the acquisitions will be data center related. For the past three years, we deliberately wanted to focus on data center because we felt that we needed to build a position throughout the gray space and the white space.
We have targeted a number of spaces where we wanted to be, cooling, testing, medium/low voltage, gensets. We also targeted a number of geographies, U.S., Europe, Asia, to make a long story short. Well, I'm not saying that we are all set, and we still have a lot of ideas of companies that could complement our setup, but we have done a lot of the job. We have a product portfolio which is a lot more comprehensive than it was three, four years back. To make a long story short, I don't believe that 100% or even 80% of acquisitions would be data center related, number one. Number two, the data center business won't grow 25%-30% every year.
We can discuss whether the growth rate long term going to be 10%, 15% or 20%, but it won't be 30% or 40%, which was the case last year. Hopefully, the building market will also rebound. You have to put all that into your model. Now, would it be a bad news for Legrand if the data center business was to be a 40%, 42%, 44%? I don't believe it would. It would, I think give us additional growth potential. From an investor standpoint, I think it would be good news more than bad news.

Martin Wilkie (Analyst, Citi): Great. Thank you very much.

Operator: Thank you. In the interest of time, please limit to one question at a time. We will now take our next question from the line of Alexander Virgo from Evercore ISI. Please go ahead.

Alexander Virgo (Analyst, Evercore ISI): Good morning, gentlemen. I wondered if you could just give us a little bit more of a sense on the North America business. I'm just trying to establish, I guess going back to some of the earlier questions, growth from data centers versus growth from non-data centers. It looks like even at 2023, your non-DC business is growing pretty well, actually. Probably a little bit stronger than I would have expected. I'm just trying to get a sense of what's driving that, the breadth of the growth in the portfolio, and then just if you could give us a little sense of color on DC in North America, that would be super helpful. Thank you.

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): Well, yes, the non-data center business is growing. The data center piece is growing more than +30%, as I said. The non-data center business is growing, and within the non-data center business, it's not resi. Everything's related to energy transition outside the resi. Again, it's all those verticals which we are now targeting, health, education, infra, industries, transportation, and so on and so forth. Complementary verticals that we have progressively added, either organically through the reallocation of some resources previously dedicated to office, or inorganically through some of the acquisitions dedicated to data center, which we have made, the Girtz and the Kratos, the Avtron, and so on. Energy transition in new verticals, which is growing nicely. As for the resi, it remains quite depressed. Again, it's 10% for U.S. sales.
As far as the office market is concerned, we are seeing no rebound to the office market. The usual KPIs we are tracking, vacancy rates, for example, or square feet being built are not really improving. We are successfully doing what we said a couple of years back we would do, i.e., we are repositioning the group in the U.S. not only into data centers, but also into other verticals than resi and office. This repositioning has some benefits.

Alexander Virgo (Analyst, Evercore ISI): Very helpful. Thank you, Benoît.

Operator: Thank you. We will now take our next question from Eric Lemarié from CIC CIB. Please go ahead, Eric. Your line is open.

Eric Lemarié (Analyst, CIC CIB): Yes. Hi, good morning. A question on data center. Do you start to see some new players coming, challenging your position, especially in the U.S., players coming from, I don't know, other businesses or other geographical area?

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): Well, not really. Well, we have new entrants which have bought some assets, especially in liquid cooling, which has been a very attractive spot to a lot of people. You could see, as I could, a couple of deals being done lately at quite healthy price on some liquid cooling assets. Otherwise, no. Data center market has always been quite competitive. As competitive as the building market, actually, in the U.S. and elsewhere. You have a lot of tough guys, either big companies or smaller ones. I haven't seen an increase in competitive intensity in data centers.

Eric Lemarié (Analyst, CIC CIB): Okay. If I may, a very quick follow-up.

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): Yeah.

Eric Lemarié (Analyst, CIC CIB): You mentioned this energy transition solution very well oriented in the U.S. Do you see the same trend in Europe? Nothing yet?

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): Yeah. It's better than essentials in Europe by a few percentage points. Well, it's not as spectacular as you can see in businesses such as HVAC because of the heat wave. For example, we are not selling air conditioning, or we are not selling a heat pump, but we are selling the back-end infrastructure that supports HVAC, heat pump, or electrification. Again, switchgear, transformers, and so on, so forth. Yes, in Europe, if we look at the -2% we are doing, actually the energy transition business is growing in Europe. We'd like it to grow more, but it's growing, whereas the essential business is down.

Eric Lemarié (Analyst, CIC CIB): Very clear. Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. We will now proceed to take our next question from Aron Ceccarelli from Bank of America. Please go ahead, Aron. Your line is open.

Aron Ceccarelli (Analyst, Bank of America): Hello, good morning. Thanks for squeezing me in. I have one on M&A. You have deployed close to around EUR 1 billion on acquisition in H1 alone. Given the increasing scarcity and valuation of quality datacenter assets, where do you still see opportunities to create value through M&A and other segments where you simply are willing to pay current market prices?

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): I don't really know what you call current market price. For Legrand, current market price are 10 times EBIT. This is price we are paying, right? If the question is, do you see more opportunities to do M&A at 10, 11, 12 times EBIT? The answer is yes. We have a number of discussions going on at this level of price. Again, we don't intend to spend EUR 1 billion per semester. We've done a lot of acquisitions for the past 18 months, so the pace will slow down by definition. We won't have a parameter impact of 8% every year. Yes, we see a lot of opportunities at very reasonable prices. Why do we have so many opportunities? It's because the model of Legrand is built this way. We have a pipeline of 350 companies that we are tracking.
We have relationship with everybody. We are paying reasonable prices, fair prices. We are very fast in executing deals. We are probably targeting animals which are probably smaller for many other players. The sort of EUR 50 million- EUR 100 million companies we are targeting are probably not in the scope of some of the other bigger than Legrand industry players. We are good at docking, and I have to say that the results of the company we acquired back in 2025 are very good, including Avtron, very good. Feel better than expected, to tell you the truth. Now there's no reason why we would slow down. There's no reason why we would stop. We will slow down in terms of pace, but we won't stop, and you should expect to see more deals coming in the quarters to come.
As far as the financial capabilities are concerned, we have a leverage at the end of June, which is 2.4 times EBITDA, which is a bit higher than our historical leverage, which was comprised between 1.5 and 2, but it's not a big deal. It remains a reasonable level of leverage. We are de-leveraging fast when we pause acquisitions, and it won't be an obstacle to do this if we think that there's a very attractive company fitting well into a setup at reasonable prices. Even with the level of leverage, we can of course do it. Yes, we will continue.

Aron Ceccarelli (Analyst, Bank of America): Thank you. If I may, just a quick follow-up on your busway business. You had a great success on developing the Starline brand to multi-million euros business. Now you acquired a smaller business in medium-voltage switchgear, Kratos, at the beginning of this year. The medium-voltage switchgear is probably a little bit more consolidated market, is less close to your core because it's medium voltage. We start to see some of the high-voltage players coming to that market as well. What does it actually take to win in MV switchgear, and do you think you are potentially able to replicate what you've done with Starline, with Kratos now?

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): I think there is a fundamental misunderstanding of what the competition in the market is, the data center market is. Take, for example, medium voltage in the U.S. You have a very few limited number of companies doing circuit breakers. You have basically the big four, which are doing medium and low voltage breakers. You have a lot of smaller companies integrating those breakers into their panels and doing highly engineered, customized, very technical panels for data center customers, but for other customers, incorporating the breakers from X, Y, or Z. Kratos is one of them. Kratos do not have its own breaker capabilities, but it's integrating third-party breakers, could be AC, could be DC, into big, big panels, which are very complicated to do, delivered within a few weeks, and serving the needs of data center customers.
This market is highly scattered. With additional active reconciliation possibilities. The one having the relationship with the end customer is Kratos. Kratos is working with the design teams of its customers on specific design, on-demand design of very technical big panels, then we'll incorporate the components from X, Y, or Z. By the way, it has very nice margins. This medium voltage market, as you call it's not one market with four big guys holding each 25%. It's a market with a number of component suppliers, some of them being the big names you know, and multiple smaller players, very good, very technical, with a strong team of engineers, very good service, sometimes on-site service to do commissioning and testing, able to incorporate those components into subsystems which are very appreciated from customers.
If the question is, do you intend to grow Kratos 20%, 30%, 40% per year? Yes, of course. It's our objective. We have designed a business plan which incorporates a lot of growth for Kratos. Since the beginning of the year, the acquisition is quite recent, but since the beginning of the year, Kratos is growing very nicely and has another book, which makes us very confident on the fact that the business plan we have designed at the time of the acquisitions will be meet or even beat, if I may say.

Aron Ceccarelli (Analyst, Bank of America): That's very helpful. Thank you very much.

Operator: Thank you. We will now take our next question from James Moore from Rothschild & Co Redburn. Please go ahead, James. Your line is open.

James Moore (Analyst, Rothschild & Co Redburn): Good morning. Thanks for the time. Benoît, you've said around 80% of the portfolio is protected from a move to 800 VDC. As AI data center architectures evolve, do you expect OCP and other emerging standards to lead to a more open multi-sourced ecosystem in which, as you said in the past, each sub-market is determined by the individual players? Do you think value is going to concentrate into a smaller number of integrated power platforms?

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): I'm not sure. I'm not sure because take OCP, for example. It's a good example. OCP, for those who are not on the market, OCP is a sort of common standard for racks which has been developed by a few hyperscalers. It's not because you have a common standard that you have commoditization or concentration of a product family. For example, you have common standards in many product family. You have common standards in jacks, you have common standards in circuit breakers, you have common standards in many things. It did not lead to a concentration of a few market players because you have a lot of different ways to add value into an OCP rack. The rack itself gives you a certain ability to design different things from one player to another.
You have the way everything is organized within the rack, and then you have the components, and so on, so forth. I don't believe that any of those architecture, neither the OCP, the AC-DC hybrid model, 800 V DC, 1,000 V DC, or whatever, will lead to a concentration of player. I think it will bring some innovation to the market. It will probably give a sort of competitive advantage to those who already have the relationship with the hyperscalers, such as we do, to those who have already a large catalog, a large portfolio of products, to those who have the technology, or if they don't have it in-house, who have the supply chain to onboard easy this technology from third party. That's why I'm very confident in our ability to be part of the new architecture.
Again, 100% of the orders everybody gets today, not only Legrand, but everybody gets on this market are based on the traditional AC architecture. 100%. Even the orders which should be delivered in 2027, 2028. It's not for today. It would be a good news because the more added value you bring to an architecture, the more ability we have to sell products. Again, the penetration rate by 2030, which is within four years, would still be limited. Core assumption, I remind you what I said at the beginning of the call. Core assumption is 10%-20% for hybrid, a few percent for LVDC.

James Moore (Analyst, Rothschild & Co Redburn): Very clear. Could I just follow up with one clarification or follow up on sidecar? Where specifically do you gain or lose content? Is the incremental opportunity primarily existing products, busway, protection, distribution, or is it entirely new product categories that you're now designing and might launch in Singapore or the likes?

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): For us, it's mostly additional value. For the players who are in UPS, you would argue that with the sort of disaggregation of the end of the powertrain within the white space, this architecture needs no UPS but this additional object, which is a sidecar. I was telling you that we were a significant U.S. player, but unfortunately, not in data centers. Right. We are a significant UPS player, but not in data centers. We are a significant UPS player elsewhere, in commercial buildings, in health, hospitals and hospitality, and so on and so forth. But in data centers, we've not really been able yet to enter the UPS space. We have almost nothing to lose because we're not selling UPS. We have only to gain because there's this new object, which is a sidecar.
It includes a number of components which we can either develop ourselves or once again source. Even in a powertrain, we're not doing all components. Even in a rack, we are not doing all components. We can either develop or buy. It will mostly be an additional value for Legrand. Again, welcome to Singapore.

James Moore (Analyst, Rothschild & Co Redburn): Look forward to it. Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. Due to time constraints, kindly limit yourselves to one question. We will now take our next question. The question comes from Ben Uglow from Oxcap Analytics. Please go ahead, Ben. Your line is open.

Ben Uglow (Analyst, Oxcap Analytics): Yeah. Morning, guys. Thank you for taking the question. It's a slightly blunt follow-up on some of the earlier discussions. What I'm trying to understand is not the direction, but the magnitude on the European margin. 18% is the lowest level we've seen on your European margin since that COVID quarter, and that was against a completely different volume backdrop. Benoît, you talked about, I think maybe I understood it, but bearing maybe more central costs. We talked a little bit about volume. But if we had to simplify, is this about just pricing and price cost? Is the bulk of that gap coming from price cost? Am I right to assume that the majority of that will be alleviated in the second half? Just understanding why it's down there, please.

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): Sure. Well, we'll let Franck take the question then.

Franck Lemery (CFO, Legrand): Yeah.

Ben Uglow (Analyst, Oxcap Analytics): Thank you.

Franck Lemery (CFO, Legrand): Yes, Ben. It's very consistent with what Benoît said earlier. The 18%, if it were to be compared to last year, it's close to -5 points. It's low, but the 5 points gross margin is holding well. SG&A, with the pattern of Europe, it's not a question of adaptation, it's just some costs are located in Europe. SG&A is - 30 basis points roughly. You have other operating items, - 140, especially with the exceptional restructuring that we already quoted and which is very legitimate in Europe. Look at our sales. It's a legitimate adaptation with restructuring, which will deliver paybacks in the further future. On the gross margin side, Europe is doing the job in terms of pricing versus inflation.

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): It's mostly SG&A, which are a bit more fixed than elsewhere and also a number of central costs which will not cut because the European volumes are going down. Restructuring, you may have heard, Ben, for example, that we are closing four sites in France. Even in a country like France, which tends to be a bit more sensitive than elsewhere, we are closing sites because we feel that we should continue to adapt to the reality of the building market, which is not yet recovering.

Ben Uglow (Analyst, Oxcap Analytics): Understood. Thank you very much. I'll pass it on in the interest of time.

Operator: Thank you. We will now take our next question from the line of William Mackie from Kepler Cheuvreux. Please go ahead, William. Your line is open.

William Mackie (Analyst, Kepler Cheuvreux): Yeah, good morning. Thank you for making the time. Perhaps I'll just have the one question as a top-down conceptual. You've upgraded your organic growth guidance significantly, but you've left your operating profit expectations flat. How would you characterize the implied lack of operational gearing when you think about the various buckets, including mix evolution, cost and price realization?

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): Well, we did not expect when we entered the year, to have leverage, even though we're shooting not for 8 to 10, but we're already shooting for significant organic growth increase. You have different brackets where you have, well, number one, the dilution from acquisitions, even if limited. We expect to have slightly dilutive impact on the margin from acquisitions in 2026. Number two, we have adjusted our price, as you know, and our target is as usual, to compensate in value the increase in purchase price through pricing. It can have a slight negative impact on margin. It's not a problem. In compensating in value, not necessarily in margin, where we have the one-off cost, which remains significant because we intend to keep doing a restructuring.
We have also all the inefficiencies that come with the strong growth we are experiencing in data center, which is difficult to quantify, which to be very candid, which we haven't quantified. When you have a big customer asking your products to be delivered on site next week.
Sometimes you are doing plane instead of a ship. Altogether, this 8%-10% of organic growth or this 16%-19% total growth will translate into a margin between 20.5% and 21%, which is not that bad, which remains at a good level. Does it mean that we are not doing productivity? The answer is no. I can share with you an interesting number for H1. Our volume is up by close to 7% in H1. Like for like, number of people is flat. Yes, we are doing productivity and we intend to keep doing productivity. This is one of the reasons why we have significant exception rules, at the same time, we have a dilution in efficiencies, purchase pricing fixing, and so on and so forth.

William Mackie (Analyst, Kepler Cheuvreux): Thank you. Specifically going back to the follow-up on the last question.

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): Yeah.

William Mackie (Analyst, Kepler Cheuvreux): Your SG&A expense in Europe was up EUR 50 million quarter-on-quarter, Q2 on last year, against less growth in Europe on revenue. How should we think about that? Is that a new base, or should we think that there were some one-time charges for repositioning or provisioning or reserving, which will reverse as we go into the second half of the year?

Franck Lemery (CFO, Legrand): Globally speaking, all that is more or less run rate with dedicated investment, for example, in R&D, in digital. All that is preparing the future. There is just a single one-timer, which is the employee shareholder plan, which is hitting only Q2. The total amount for that is a little above EUR 10 million for the group. I will not disclose the number for Europe alone, but this is for the group. This is the only one-timer, or otherwise, as I said, we keep investing for the group in Europe. We are managing the total P&L. There's a couple of questions on the margin in Europe. Is the margin in Europe a problem for Legrand? The answer is no. Clearly, we manage the margin at group level.
Whether we have a little bit more restructuring here, a little bit less here, because we are closing site in France and maybe not in the U.S., and opening site in the U.S. Whether the R&D costs are in China or in India. All that for us, it's, as we say in French, right pocket, left pocket. What matter is the margin we are able to have at group level. Again, with 20.5%-21%, it's a very healthy level of margin. The priority, to make things clear, the priority for more than two years now has been put on delivering more growth, and especially more organic growth. We feel that there is a historical opportunity for Legrand to accelerate its top-line potential, which has been stuck at 1%-3% for years.
We've been able to reposition the group towards data center energy transition, and our objective is to grow the group as fast as possible while maintaining a satisfactory level of margin and a satisfactory level of free cash flow. It has been the target. The target has not been to improve margin for the past couple of years. This is a deliberate decision, and I think it's in the interest of our customers and our shareholders. William, I did not mention because I hope it's clear for you, the number you quoted is not on a like for like basis, huh? It's including acquisitions. We have consolidated a few acquisitions in Europe. Organically, in Europe, we have gross margin, which is a bit under pressure as elsewhere, but nothing significant. We're able to pass on the same price.
We have SG&A which are not adjusted as much as you could think of for two reasons. A few one-off, like the sharing plan, but it's not big cost. Number two, because it bears a lot of central costs, R&D, management, AI, and so on and so forth. Last, more restructuring, because we are closing a number of sites in order to keep optimizing our footprint. Nothing to be worried about. That's it.

William Mackie (Analyst, Kepler Cheuvreux): Very clear. Thank you.

Operator: That's the end of the question and answer session. Thank you all very much for your questions. I'll now turn the conference back to Mr. Coquart for his closing comments.

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): Well, thank you very much for your time, and for your questions. Should you have more questions, you have the whole team at your disposal to answer. And for those of you who are lucky enough to take a summer break, I wish you a good and relaxing break. Thanks a lot.

Operator: Thank you for your participation in today's conference. This does conclude the program. You may now disconnect your line.

Operator: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen, and welcome to today's Legrand's 2026 half year results conference call. For your information, this conference is being recorded. All participants are in a listen-only mode. Later, there will be a question-and-answer session. At this time, I would like to hand the call over to CEO, Mr. Benoît Coquart, and CFO, Mr. Franck Lemery. Please go ahead, sir.

Benoît Coquart (CEO, Legrand): Thank you very much. Good morning, everybody. Franck, Renaud, and myself are happy to welcome you to Legrand H1 2026 conference call and webcast. This morning, as usual, we published our press release, financial statements, and the slideshow that we will refer to during the call. After a few opening remarks, we will comment on the results in more details. Let me start on page four with the key highlights of the quarter. First, Legrand delivered another period of record sales growth together with continued excellent profitability. Second, we are continuing to implement our 2030 strategic roadmap with determination. Third, we are raising our full year 2026 targets. Moving to pages six and seven, I will start with an overview of sales. Sales delivered strong growth of +17.4% in H1 2026, excluding currency effect, comprising first, an organic growth of +9.8%, driven by data centers and energy transition-related offerings.
Second, growth from acquisitions with a positive scope effect of +6.9%. Based on acquisitions announced and the likely date of consolidation, the overall impact of acquisitions would be around +8% for the full year. The exchange rate effect was -3.7% in H1. Based on average exchange rates in June 2026, the full-year currency effect would be around -1.5%. On page seven, you will find the key takeaways by geographies on a like-for-like basis. Europe saw sales down -2.4% in a building market that remains as expected contrasted. North and Central America increased sharply by +24.2%, driven by strong success of data center and energy transition solutions in the U.S. Lastly, rest of the world grew by +2.3% in the first half, with significant growth in India, Australia, and several other Asian countries, while activity in China remained soft.
